metadata.title: Why Do Language Models Hallucinate?
metadata.note: STEM/AI topic-of-interest video on LLM hallucination, kept factually grounded rather than anthropomorphizing. Covers: hallucination is confident, fluent generation of unsupported claims, not intentional deception or self-aware error; the root cause is that next-token prediction optimizes for plausible/fluent continuation, not verified truth, and nothing in the base generation loop checks facts; practical mitigations that reduce but do not eliminate the problem (retrieval-grounding, requesting citations); the honest limit that a confident tone is never proof of accuracy, so high-stakes claims still need independent verification. Built using the same proven pattern set as prior videos: folderLabel set explicitly on ClaudeComposerAsk beats (@HumanitariansAI), OutroCTA used instead of ClaudeTitleOutro, BLUF lines kept short to avoid edge-bleed, no stale sparse_by_design flags except the legitimate BrutalistHesitantWriter typing-beat exemption.

skin_warnings: B08: palette=claude but the outro is 'OutroCTA' — OUTRO LAW wants ClaudeTitleOutro

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — HAI persona, world-language hello (short form only)
beats.narration_text: Hi. Why does a language model sometimes state something false with total confidence?

props.command: claude "explain why language models produce confident, fluent, but factually wrong answers, and what actually reduces it"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. A model should be able to tell when it doesn't actually know something. That sounds like a reasonable expectation. It isn't that simple — the model is built to sound right, not built to check that it is right.

props.text:
A model should know what it doesn't know.
That sounds like a reasonable expectation.
It isn't. It's built to sound right.

qc.sparse_reason: hesitant-writer typing bookend accumulates one line token by token — mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design (documented exemption case in final_frame_check.py)

beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat
beats.narration_text: This isn't the model lying on purpose. There's no awareness of the falsehood, no intent to deceive. It's confident guessing — fluent, well formed text, presented the same way whether the underlying claim is true or completely made up.
beats.visual_intent: two cards contrasting the sci-fi framing with what's actually happening

items.label: Not Lying
items.sub: no intent, no awareness of falsehood

beats.visual_intent: simple description card explaining the root cause
beats.narration_text: Here's the actual mechanism. A model predicts the next likely word, not a verified fact. Its training data has gaps and contradictions. Producing fluent, plausible text is the real objective — and nothing built into that process checks the result against reality before it's shown to you.

lines: Models predict the next likely word, not truth.
Training data has gaps and contradictions.
Fluent, plausible text is the actual goal.
Nothing built-in checks facts before output.

beats.narration_text: As a pipeline: a prompt comes in. The model predicts plausible text, one piece at a time. There's no fact-check step in that loop. In longer answers, small errors can compound on each other. The result is a confident answer that was never actually verified.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram ending at an unverified claim, not a checked fact

props.title: Fluent Isn't the Same as True
props.footerNote: nothing in this loop checks the claim against reality
props.sparkLine: Fluent isn't the same as true.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here
beats.narration_text: Here's what genuinely reduces this. Grounding a model's answer in real, retrieved sources — rather than letting it generate from memory alone — cuts down on invented claims. Asking for citations does something similar: it forces a claim to be checkable, not just confident.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page showing the two concrete mitigations

items.label: Asking for Citations
items.sub: makes a claim checkable, not just confident

beats.role_note: the lesson, honest about scope — this is where the real limitation lives
beats.narration_text: But here's the catch that matters. These methods reduce hallucination — they don't eliminate it. A confident, fluent tone is never proof that something is accurate. For anything high-stakes, the claim still needs independent verification, not just a convincing delivery.

lines: These reduce hallucination, not eliminate it.
A confident tone is never proof of accuracy.
Trust the check, not the tone.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — ClaudeComposerAsk, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.', prompt read and discussed aloud
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Don't trust a confident tone on its own. Ask Claude to ground its answer in real sources, or to flag clearly what it isn't sure about, instead of stating everything the same way.

props.command:
claude "ground this answer in real sources, and
clearly flag anything you're not fully sure about
instead of stating it as fact"
